newsitem.title: EGYPT: Peace depends on Israel fulfilling deals - Egypt.
newsitem.headline: Peace depends on Israel fulfilling deals - Egypt.

text.p: Egypt said on Friday the future of Middle East peace talks rested solely in the hands of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and denied Egypt had incited the Palestinians to delay an agreement on the town of Hebron.

President Hosni Mubarak told a joint news conference with visiting French President Jacques Chirac that Israel would cause "a big disaster" if it failed to carry out agreements it signed with the Palestinians before Netanyahu came to office.
Chirac said he fully agreed with Mubarak's analysis of the causes of what he called the crisis in Middle East peace talks.
"The solution is in the hands of the prime minister of Israel alone -- it's to stick to what's been agreed. We are not asking for a miracle," Mubarak said.
Otherwise all Israel's agreements with its neighbours, such as Egypt and Jordan, would be in doubt and Middle East governments would be anxious and hesitant, he added.

"If another government comes and says, 'No. we won't play this game", it will be a disaster. My God! So then the Labour Party might come and say: 'No, we don't agree with the Likud. Give back the Golan, give back Sinai, or give back the West Bank', then it would be a big disaster," he added.
"One day he (Netanyahu) could break with us what we signed in the days of (former Israeli prime minister Menachem) Begin. He could break the agreement with Jordan," he said.
Mubarak said that during recent negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians over Hebron, Israelis had spread rumours that Egypt was holding the Palestinians back.

Israel was meant to redeploy its troops from the West Bank town more than a year ago but Netanyahu's rightwing government is trying to renegotiate the terms on the grounds of providing more security for Jewish settlers there.

"The prime minister of Israel told me: 'Arafat doesn't want to solve the problem and I understand he wants to delay and I don't know who told him to do it.' I told him, no it's a rumour which you put out," Mubarak said.

"Arafat has not turned his brain off and doesn't wait for us to tell him to agree or not to agree. Arafat has full responsibility to sign what he wants and he is responsible to his people, not to Egypt," he added.
Chirac, who spent about 90 minutes with Mubarak on the last stop of his six-day tour of the Middle East, said:

"Yes, we (France and Egypt) have an identity of views on the causes of the crisis. President Mubarak has just spoken of the consequences which must be avoided...the anxieties one might have. On all that, we have an identity of views."
Chirac said that after his tour, which sought to give France and Europe a higher profile in Middle East peace negotiations, he had a better idea of the role men of peace could play.
"I've seen what messages one could pass, either disceetly or officially, to try to improve things a little," he added.
Mubarak volunteered Egypt's view that the main mediator must remain the United States though Europe could also help.
"President Clinton is making great efforts... He has insisted that the peace process must continue," he added.

Chirac, in a retort to domestic critics of the attention he has given to the Middle East, told the news conference that France's trade surplus hit a historic high of 13.9 billion francs ($2.7 billion) in August. Most of this came through an increase in exports to Europe and the Middle East, he said.
"It is not unconnected with the determination of French diplomacy to submit itself to the service of employment in our country," he added.
"I have also tried to defend the interests of France, as I have done ever since I was elected, and I underline to you that the results have been not at all negligible," he said.
